prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
The Python Software Foundation and CPython developers have outlined specific performance expectations and trade-offs for the free-threaded (no-GIL) build through PEP 703, PEP 779, and official documentation. The consensus is that while single-threaded performance incurs a penalty due to thread-safety overhead, this is an acceptable cost for enabling true parallelism in multi-threaded applications.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)." | CLAIM: Current benchmarks indicate a roughly 10% performance penalty for single-threaded workloads on Linux and Windows, and 3% on macOS.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "We propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: The proposed hard target for acceptable performance degradation in phase II of free-threading support is 15%.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds." | CLAIM: Disabling the GIL inherently increases execution overhead due to the necessary thread-safety mechanisms.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non `--disable-gil`) builds of CPython." | CLAIM: The standard GIL-enabled build of CPython will not suffer any performance regression from the changes introduced to support free-threading.

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official documentation states that single-threaded overhead varies by platform, ranging from 1% on macOS ARM to 8% on Linux x86-64.

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council initially expected a worst-case performance penalty between 10% and 15%.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)." | CLAIM: In addition to CPU overhead, the free-threaded build currently consumes 15-20% more memory on average.
